bib.title: Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?

read.skipped: Reference list (lines ~1001-1350) skimmed only. The PDF is arXiv v3 (1 Oct 2024) and prints no venue; EMNLP 2024 comes from the repo's references, not from the PDF.

question: Does fine-tuning an LLM on examples that introduce facts it did not learn in pre-training make it hallucinate more about facts it already knows?
hypothesis: A common conjecture (Schulman 2023 and others) that exposure to new knowledge in fine-tuning encourages hallucination; the paper tests it and does not state a prediction of its own.
contributions: SliCK, a four-category taxonomy (HighlyKnown, MaybeKnown, WeaklyKnown, Unknown) of facts relative to a model's knowledge, built from sampled PCorrect
A controlled closed-book QA study varying the Unknown share of a fixed-size fine-tuning set
Findings: Unknown examples are fit slowly, fitting them lowers accuracy roughly linearly, and MaybeKnown examples matter most

method.summary: Annotate every ENTITYQUESTIONS train example as HighlyKnown, MaybeKnown, WeaklyKnown or Unknown for PaLM 2-S using 10 random 4-shot prompts (1 greedy and 16 T=0.5 samples each). Full fine-tune PaLM 2-S for 50 epochs on fixed-size (6142) datasets with X% Unknown, evaluate every epoch, and compare early-stop with convergence.
method.task: closed-book question answering on (subject, relation, object) triplets turned into questions

datasets.name: ENTITYQUESTIONS (Sciavolino et al., 2021)
datasets.size: 81700 annotated train examples over 12 relations (Table 4); fine-tuning set |D| = 6142; in-distribution test 10481 (Table 5); OOD test 5848 over 7 relations (Table 6)
datasets.split: original train/dev/test splits; train sub-sampled to build D variants
datasets.source: Wikidata triplets converted to QA pairs
datasets.preprocessing: 12 relations randomly sampled for train/dev/test; 5 of the 12 reserved relations dropped for similarity to train relations, leaving 7 OOD relations; examples with more than 1 correct answer removed (4.2% of train, 3.9% of test); subject/object overlap between train and test removed (2.1% of train removed).

other.note: S is the middle of five sizes (XXS, XS, S, M, L); parameter count not given

training.objective: supervised fine-tuning on (question, answer) pairs; prompt format 'Answer the following question.\n<question>'
training.lr_schedule: inferred: fixed (constant) learning rate, paper says 'a fixed learning rate'
training.epochs: 50 for every variant; evaluated on dev every epoch; EARLY_STOP = epoch of max dev accuracy (5-10 epochs); CONVERGENCE = epoch 50 (100% train accuracy)
training.compute: Not given in GPU-hours. Annotation alone took 170 inference steps per example, more than 15M inference steps for the full dataset.

other.variants: X% Unknown with the rest Known, fixed |D|=6142, relation distribution kept constant; single-category variants D_HighlyKnown, D_MaybeKnown, D_WeaklyKnown, D_Unknown and D_Natural; D_Known ablations with Unknown filtered out; D_IDK relabels Unknown answers as 'I don't know'

inference.decoding: greedy for evaluation (inferred: exact-match test accuracy); annotation uses 1 greedy (T=0) plus 16 samples at T=0.5 per prompt
inference.samples: Annotation: Nex=10 random 4-shot prompts x (1 greedy + Nsample=16 sampled) per example. Fine-tuning: no seeds or repeated runs stated.
inference.prompting: 4-shot with exemplars from the dev split, same relation as the question (Q:/A: format)

metrics.name: Exact match accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of test questions whose predicted answer exactly matches the gold answer; used as a proxy for hallucination w.r.t. pre-existing knowledge because train and test are disjoint

metrics.name: Accuracy on answered questions and % answered
metrics.definition: for the 'I don't know' variant, accuracy on test questions where the model did not abstain, and the share it answered

baselines: fine-tuning on D with the Known categories only (D_Known)
P(True) (Kadavath et al., 2022) as an alternative Unknown detector
eval.protocol: Single PaLM 2-S, one run per variant. Table 2 significance: test set shuffled into 100 subsets, paired-sample t-test at p<0.05 and p<0.01. Linear model (Eq. 1) fitted on (Accuracy, N_Kn, N_Unk) collected after each epoch from all D variants.

availability.data: ENTITYQUESTIONS is public; the SliCK annotations are not stated as released

evidence.quote: We use learning rate of 1e-5, a batch size of 128, and a dropout rate of 0.05.

results.claim: Test accuracy is linearly predicted by the number of Known and Unknown fine-tuning examples the model fits; fitting Unknown hurts and fitting Known helps by a similar amount.
results.unit: accuracy points per unit fraction of |D| fit
results.setup: PaLM 2-S, ENTITYQUESTIONS in-distribution test, points collected after each epoch from all D variants; Eq. 1 valid only for N_kn<=|D|, N_unk<=|D|. beta_0=36.9, beta_kn=7.3, R2=0.86.
results.note: Text prints the symbol as beta_ukn in one place.

results.claim: Same linear model on the out-of-distribution relations has smaller coefficients and a better fit.
results.setup: 7 OOD relations unseen in fine-tuning; beta_0=36.2, beta_kn=3.2, beta_unk=-3.0.

results.claim: Unknown examples are fit much more slowly than Known ones; at the best dev point the model has fit most Known but few Unknown examples.
results.setup: 50% Known / 50% Unknown D, PaLM 2-S. Only read from Fig 1, no text number.
results.quote: The best development performance is obtained when the LLM fits the majority of the Known training examples but only few of the Unknown ones.

results.claim: With early stopping, removing Unknown examples changes almost nothing, but at convergence they are very harmful and the gap grows with the Unknown share.
results.setup: Fixed |D|=6142, X% Unknown, EARLY_STOP (5-10 epochs) vs CONVERGENCE (50 epochs). Numbers only in Fig 3.
results.quote: Conversely, the CONVERGENCE results show that with longer training, Unknown examples are actually very harmful.

results.claim: Re-labelling Unknown fine-tuning answers as 'I don't know' keeps accuracy on answered questions at 61.8 at both early stop and convergence, at the cost of answering fewer questions.
results.setup: 50% Known / 50% Unknown variant only. % answered for D_IDK was 58.7 at EARLY_STOP and 55.6 at CONVERGENCE; D answers 100%.
results.quote: Specifically, the accuracy for DIDK re-mains 61.8 for both EARLY_STOP and CONVERGENCE, with a small decrease on the number of willingly answered questions (58.7 →55.6).
results.note: The 61.8 is accuracy on the answered subset, not on all test questions, so it is not directly comparable with D's 43.0 over 100% answered.

results.claim: Fine-tuning only on HighlyKnown examples is not best; MaybeKnown examples give the best overall accuracy and the best MaybeKnown-test accuracy.
results.setup: Single-category variants, |D|=6142. D_MaybeKnown 69.9 vs D_HighlyKnown 60.1 on MaybeKnown test examples; HighlyKnown test 98.4 vs 98.7. D_Natural 43.5.
results.quote: Compared to DHighlyKnown, DMaybeKnown enhances MD’s performance on MaybeKnown (60.1→69.9), without compromising performance on HighlyKnown (98.7 →98.4).
results.table: Table 2, row D_MaybeKnown, column EARLY_STOP Full

results.claim: Training the Unknown-only variant to convergence collapses overall accuracy, with large losses on facts the model already knew.
results.setup: D_Unknown, CONVERGENCE vs EARLY_STOP; on HighlyKnown test examples 95.6 falls to 55.8. D_WeaklyKnown falls 39.2 to 35.4.
results.quote: Specifically, at CONVERGENCE, DWeaklyKnown and DUnknown expe-rience significant performance drops compared to EARLY_STOP (39.2 →35.4 and 37.5 →25.8).

results.claim: SliCK Unknown test examples really are unknown: accuracy after fine-tuning on them is tiny.
results.metric: post-fine-tuning accuracy on Unknown test subset
results.quote: In Table 2 we can see that the accuracy on Unknown is extremely low (3.2% or less), which is a strong indicator that most of the Unknown examples are actually unknown to M.

results.claim: Category mix of ENTITYQUESTIONS for PaLM 2-S: 36% Unknown, 24% HighlyKnown.
results.setup: 12 relations, PaLM 2-S, 10 prompts x (1 greedy + 16 samples).
results.quote: In ENTITYQUESTIONS we have 24% HighlyKnown, 23% MaybeKnown, 17%, WeaklyKnown, and 36% Unknown.

results.claim: The out-of-distribution accuracy drop from Unknown examples is smaller than in-distribution but follows the same trend.
results.setup: OOD test of 7 relations; Fig 8 vs Fig 3.
results.quote: We no-tice that similar trends, just with a smaller overall magnitude of the performance drop, up to 6 points drop compared to up to 14 for in-distribution.

results.claim: Using fewer than 10 few-shot prompts to estimate PCorrect labels Unknown examples that later get higher accuracy, and P(True) thresholding is worse than SliCK.
results.setup: Accuracy after fine-tuning with D_Natural on test examples classed Unknown. The authors call it preliminary.
results.quote: Lastly, the blue line shows that using samples from mul-tiple few-shot prompts to approximate PCorrect is crucial, as using Nex < 10 leads to higher test accuracy on SliCK Unknown examples.

results.claim: In 100 inspected exact-match failures of the pre-trained model, 90 were truly wrong answers.
results.setup: 50 greedy plus 50 T=0.5 predictions; 6% paraphrase, 2% higher granularity, 2% lower granularity.
results.quote: This analysis suggest that in 90% of the cases where EM is False, the predicted answer is indeed incorrect.

limits: Single LLM (PaLM 2-S); authors say replication on more models is very compute-heavy.
Closed-book short-answer QA only; filtering Unknown examples is not validated for long-form generation.
No mix of other task types added to fine-tuning, so it does not match typical instruction tuning.
Full fine-tuning only; LoRA and continual pretraining untested. Findings on offline preference optimisation such as DPO left for future work.
No seeds, repeated runs or error bars for the fine-tuning runs; significance tests only split the test set.
Accuracy drop is used as a proxy for hallucination and cannot separate forgetting from hallucination (footnote 17).
SliCK is an approximation; at most about 3% of Unknown examples may actually be known.
The 'I don't know' result is one setting (50% Unknown); the P(True) comparison is preliminary.
The linear model is valid only in a bounded region (N_kn <= |D|, N_unk <= |D|).
The optimizer, warmup, hardware, sequence length and precision are not given, and no code or weights are stated.
